canonical_name: Philip K. Dick and the Bible
definition: Philip K. Dick's engagement with the Bible across his life: a familiar text before 1974, then, after the experiences of February and March 1974, the principal framework through which he interpreted them — read as a book of the future, a cipher, a living organism, and a source his own novels had unknowingly reproduced.
pkd_relevance: No text appears more often in the Exegesis or does more work there. Acts, Daniel, Revelation, Malachi, the Wisdom of Solomon, John and 1 Corinthians each supply a structural idea: the Empire, Elijah's return, Holy Wisdom, the Logos, impaired sight and agape.
in_the_fiction: Overtly in VALIS, The Divine Invasion, The Transmigration of Timothy Archer and Deus Irae; by Dick's later account covertly in Flow My Tears (Acts), Ubik (the Logos) and A Scanner Darkly (1 Corinthians 13).
in_the_exegesis: From 1975 to 1981: the Bible as a book of the future, as code, as living information, and as the record of which God he had met.
intellectual_background: The Septuagint and its apocrypha; Philo's allegorical Torah; the Dead Sea Scrolls and Nag Hammadi codices; the Jehovah's Witnesses' apocalyptic reading of Daniel; modern esoteric readings such as The Decoded New Testament.
scholarly_debate: Whether Dick knew Acts before 1974; how far 1 Corinthians 13 structures the fiction; the open versus the frozen scripture of The Divine Invasion.
chronology_summary: Junior high: the Elijah radio serial. 1962–73: Corinthians, King James, rhymed couplets, the Scanner Darkly title, comparing translations. 1975: Acts and Flow My Tears; the Bible as a book of the future; the Wisdom of Solomon. 1976: the Bible as code. 1978–80: living scripture; new scriptures needed. 1980–81: the Torah in Hertz's edition; the turn to Judaism and back. 1981: YHWH; the Bible as a world; recombinant scripture and a third testament; the Jerusalem Bible.
contradictions_summary: Ten, kept rather than resolved: his prior knowledge of the Bible; whether he had read Acts (in his own words, both ways); Butler against the record; the Bible dispensable or alive; code or incomplete code; which God; the Old Testament scorned or revered; Judaism or Christianity; Bishop Archer as Christ figure or lawyer; one Jason or two.
editorial_notes: Every card was chosen and summarised by reading the passage. Machine-extracted claims about the Bible in the database are unreviewed and not used. Fiction passages are characters speaking (lane A); the Exegesis is lane B; scholarship lane C; biography lane D; letters and interviews lane E.
open_questions: Which Bible did Dick own before 1974? — raised under Before 1974. Letters show the King James, the New World Translation and the New English Bible by 1973, but no inventory of his books survives in this archive. Resolvable by: an inventory of his library.

Did Dick know Acts before 1974? — raised under 1975. He says both that he had never read it and that he may have read it and forgotten. Resolvable by: pre-1974 letters outside the Selected Letters, or annotations in his own Bible.

Where did the "Ruah" interview remark and the Davis talk on the Acts of Thomas come from? — cited by the earlier Bible study but not found in this archive's texts. Resolvable by: locating those transcripts.

Was the Wisdom of Solomon letter of September 1975 sent to more than one person? — the same text is recorded once in the Exegesis ("Dear Doris") and once in the Selected Letters ("Dear Sherri"). Resolvable by: the original manuscripts.

What is Dick's source for Philo's living Torah? — raised under Living scripture. He copies a passage in quotation marks without naming the book. Resolvable by: identifying the quotation, likely an encyclopedia article on Kabbalah or Philo.
Which Exegesis passages in section 016 belong to 1978, and which to 1980? — raised under the cautions. Resolvable by: matching each segment to the folders of the published edition.
The Book of Acts is traditionally ascribed to Luke; Dick calls it "Paul's". Slip, or a reading? — raised under 1975. Unresolved.

dossier_sections.heading: Philip K. Dick and the Bible
body: The Bible is the text Philip K. Dick argued with longest. He knew it before he believed anything about it: he dates his first reading to a junior-high radio serial about Elijah {{PKB-INT-ELIJAH}}, took the title of A Scanner Darkly from Paul in 1973 {{PKB-LET-1973B}}, and was comparing translations of Ecclesiastes and 1 Corinthians five months before the experiences of February and March 1974 {{PKB-LET-1973C}}. After 2-3-74 it became the main instrument with which he tried to understand what had happened to him.

What makes his use of it distinctive is not piety but method. He read scripture as a description of the present ("The Bible is a book of the future" {{PKB-LET-1975-CLAUDIA}}), as a cipher ("The Bible is code" {{PKB-EX-1976-ACTSPRISON}}), as a living organism — the esoteric Torah of Philo, the plasmate {{PKB-EX-1978-TORAH}} — and as a source his own novels had tapped without his knowing: Flow My Tears, he came to believe, reproduces the Acts of the Apostles {{PKB-ESS-RASCH}}. Each of these readings is held alongside the others, and several contradict each other. This page keeps them apart.

The page is organised in two ways at once. The essay below runs roughly in order, from before 1974 to 1981. The index of books and themes underneath lets you go the other way: pick Acts, Daniel, Malachi or 1 Corinthians and see every passage in the archive that turns on it, whatever its date or source. Every bracketed reference in the essay opens the card it cites. For the wider religious vocabulary — Gnosticism, Kabbalah, the mystery religions — the Religion browse pages list every tagged passage; this page is the Bible's own.

dossier_sections.heading: Before 1974: a reader, not yet a believer
body: Dick's own account starts in junior high school, with The Light of the World, a daytime radio dramatisation of the Bible. He came in during the Elijah episodes, went and read the story, and wanted above all to hear the voice Elijah hears on Mount Horeb {{PKB-INT-ELIJAH}}. A schoolfriend remembered the same years differently — an atheist who could not prove God existed and who also tried to start a Bible Club {{PKB-SCH-SUTIN-02}}. The two accounts agree on the date.

The letters of the 1960s and early 1970s show a writer for whom the Bible is common property. In 1962 he describes coming out of years of agoraphobic misperception in Paul's words: he "did see face to face" {{PKB-LET-1962}}. In 1964 the King James Bible is his example of a grand style that cannot make imitation serious {{PKB-LET-1964}}; three weeks earlier he had passed on his priest's saying that the Bible "is not the story of man's search for God but of God's search for man", a formula he later gave to a character in Deus Irae {{PKB-LET-1964-PRIEST}} {{PKB-FIC-DEUSIRAE}}. In 1972–73 a dream about setting the Bible into rhymed couplets becomes a running joke with friends {{PKB-LET-1972}} {{PKB-LET-1973A}}.

Two documents from 1973 show more than familiarity. In March he explains to Carol Carr that the title of the novel he is writing, A Scanner Darkly, is a pun on 1 Corinthians 13:12 {{PKB-LET-1973B}}. In September he sets three translations of 1 Corinthians 15:51 side by side for his agent and prefers the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation as "so direct, so—honest" {{PKB-LET-1973C}}. Ubik, written years earlier, already ends its chapter epigraphs with a product that speaks as the Word of John's Gospel {{PKB-FIC-UBIK}}. He confirmed the Scanner title's source in interview {{PKB-INT-SCANNERTITLE}}, and in April 1981 he wrote that the Bible he first read in junior high "was the O.T. that I read, not the N.T., esp. the part about Elijah" {{PKB-EX-1981-FIRSTREAD}}.

This matters because Dick later said the opposite. In 1976 he told his mother that when he saw the Iron Empire in 1974 "I was almost totally unfamiliar with the Bible" {{PKB-LET-1976-HUDNER}}. The claim makes his visions independent of his reading; his own letters do not support it, at least for the Bible as a whole. In 1977 he gave a third version: his formal knowledge of Christianity was limited until March 1974, after which he read the New Testament "again and again" {{PKB-LET-1977-WARREN}}. The contradiction is recorded below rather than resolved.

dossier_sections.heading: 1975: Acts and Flow My Tears
body: The discovery that organised the rest arrived in 1975. Dick's earliest dated statement of it in this archive is a July letter to Göran Bengtson: Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said "on close inspection, contains a number of passages evidently derived from or which refer to the" Book of Acts, which he connects to a theory that his unconscious is an Attic Greek {{PKB-LET-1975-BENGTSON}}. The day before, describing the novel he was planning, he had made its climax the moment "foretold in the Bible" when the graves open {{PKB-LET-1975-GRAVES}}. To Claudia Bush he reads the novel's closing embrace between Felix Buckman and a black stranger as the Feast of Agape, and does not know how it got in {{PKB-LET-CLAUDIA-AGAPE}}.

The public telling came in the 1978 speech How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later. His Episcopalian priest, hearing the gas-station scene described, recognised it as Philip meeting the Ethiopian in Acts 8 {{PKB-ESS-RASCH}}. Dick then found Felix, the Roman official who interrogates Paul, and a single Jason sheltering a fugitive — an inversion of his own Jason Taverner {{PKB-ESS-JASON}}. In the Exegesis the name Felix becomes a key: it "points to the Biblical nature of the dream" {{PKB-EX-1975-FELIX}}.

Over the following years the Acts parallel grows from coincidence into doctrine. Acts is "a police state" and "how it really is" {{PKB-EX-1976-ACTSPRISON}}; the canonical Acts "leaves out crucial information" that survives only in the novel {{PKB-EX-1976-OMITS}}; the novel carries "unmistakable material from Acts" {{PKB-EX-1976-TEARSACTS}}, and "the true world is that of Acts", the last period of scripture {{PKB-EX-1976-TRUEWORLD}}; the recipient of the revelation lives in reality "as interpreted through + by the Acts lens/grid", a contemporary of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-CONTEMPORARY}}. By April 1981 the world he saw in 1974 is "specifically Acts - the 2nd half of Luke" {{PKB-EX-1981-LUKEACTS}}.

Had he read Acts before? He gives both answers. In the summer of 1978 he writes flatly, "I had never read Acts", and credits Father Rasch with the first clue {{PKB-EX-1978-NEVERREAD}} — then puzzles over how he could have recognised the Acts elements the month the novel came out if he had not recognised them when he wrote it {{PKB-EX-1978-RECOGNITION}}. In another entry of the same years he allows that he may have read Acts and forgotten it, and rests his case instead on material he could not have known {{PKB-EX-1978-UNCONSCIOUS}}.

dossier_sections.heading: A book of the future: Daniel, Revelation and the Empire
body: On 27 February 1975 Dick wrote the sentence that governs his apocalyptic reading: "The Bible is a book of the future." The New Testament and the Old Testament oracles are "about tomorrow"; the backdrop is familiar, the events new {{PKB-LET-1975-CLAUDIA}}. Daniel and Revelation, "the two apocalyptic books", become the lens for the tyranny he believed he had seen thrown down in 1974.

The identifications are explicit and they move. Revelation's beast is Rome, and its fall is the Parousia {{PKB-EX-1975-REVROME}}. With the Jehovah's Witnesses he reads Daniel's statue with feet of clay as the Anglo-American Empire {{PKB-EX-1975-CLAYFEET}}. By 1976 the scene is Cyrus's siege of Babylon, with Daniel the prisoner, and the equation runs Babylon = Rome = Washington DC = Moscow {{PKB-EX-1976-BABYLON}}. Apocalyptic vision, he argues, is a glimpse of eternal reality behind time, true "in Daniel's time, in John's and mine" {{PKB-EX-1975-APOC}}.

He knew how this looked. In the same 1976 sitting he copies a sociological observation from the Britannica — only the alienated yearn for divine intervention — and adds: "I fit this latter class" {{PKB-EX-1976-ALIENATED}}. In VALIS the hunt for Nixon in Daniel is given to the cynic Kevin, to Fat's amusement {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-DANIEL}}. And in October 1981, during a lightning storm, he read Revelation and Daniel to his frightened cats {{PKB-LET-1981-CATS}}.

To his mother in September 1976 he put the conclusion without irony: "the prophecies of the Bible are all true and are systematically being fulfilled" {{PKB-LET-1976-PROPHECIES}}. In November 1975 he had read the Jerusalem Bible's note calling Rome the Church's only real enemy as confirmation of what he had been shown {{PKB-EX-1975-JBIBLE}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Elijah, Malachi and the returning Spirit
body: Malachi's last chapter promises that Elijah will be sent before the great and terrible day of the Lord. Dick used it more than any other prophetic text to name what possessed him. The Lord of Hosts suddenly coming to his temple is how he describes seeing the world as a living organism {{PKB-EX-1975-MALACHI}}; the Spirit of Elijah that Malachi promises is, he decides, "the Old Testament Hebrew concept for the Christian Holy Spirit" {{PKB-EX-1975-ELIJAH}}. In 1976 he quotes the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings — and reminds himself what Elijah did to Ahab {{PKB-EX-1976-SUN}}. The ending of Malachi, he decides, shows that God foresaw Elijah's long absence and his return at the end {{PKB-EX-1976-MALACHIABSENCE}}.

The same verse appears in VALIS, where its promise of healing sharpens Fat's despair over his dying friend {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-MALACHI}}, and Elijah walks into The Divine Invasion as Elias Tate. In August 1981 the figure Dick reaches for is still the one from the radio serial: God as the "still small voice" that spoke to Elijah {{PKB-LET-1981-STILLSMALL}}. In interview he ran the identification on: "John the Baptist was Elijah", fulfilling Malachi, and the spirit of Elijah is what shows up in The Divine Invasion {{PKB-INT-BAPTIST}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Holy Wisdom from an apocryphal book
body: Dick's St. Sophia — Holy Wisdom, Hagia Sophia, the figure who becomes Zina in The Divine Invasion — came to him through a book many Protestants do not count as scripture. In September 1975 he explains to a friend that his church now recommends the apocrypha, and that the Wisdom of Solomon, part of the Septuagint the early Christians used, "was as sacred as any book of the Hebrew Scriptures" {{PKB-EX-1975-SEPTUAGINT}}.

From it he builds a theology of the Incarnation: Sophia, the world-builder of the wisdom books, entered human form and lost some of her powers while she was here {{PKB-EX-1975-WISDOM}}. By 1977 he identifies the voice in his head with "the Logos, or St. Sophia, Holy Wisdom" {{PKB-LET-1977-JAYNES}}; in 1981 Wisdom speaks in the novel as the living Torah, the blueprint of the universe {{PKB-FIC-DI-TORAH}}.

dossier_sections.heading: The Bible is code
body: The idea that scripture is a cipher appears first in fiction. In March 1975 Dick outlines a novel in which a man possessed by a Qumran Essene finds "the New Testament is in cypher" {{PKB-LET-1975-ORNSTEIN}}. By 1976 he states it about the world: the Bible "isn't about the past; it's code to describe our world", and Acts is now {{PKB-EX-1976-CODE}}. To decode it is to read the New Testament as "an encoded instruction manual by which to become part of Valis" {{PKB-EX-1976-MANUAL}}. The groundwork was laid in November 1975, when reality itself became concealed writing: "The book the Bible is an analog of reality" {{PKB-EX-1975-ANALOG}}. In the same 1976 sitting he calls Ubik a form of scripture, since "Ubik wrote 'Ubik'" {{PKB-EX-1976-UBIKSCRIPTURE}}.

The cipher has a structure. In one entry the testaments are opposing players: "O.T. encodes + N.T. decyphers", dark against light {{PKB-EX-1978-DECYPHER}}. In a darker version the cipher is technology, not revelation — an agency "using the Bible as a encoding-decoding grid" because it is printed everywhere {{PKB-EX-1978-GRID}}. In 1981 he finds the Reformers' version: the Holy Spirit hid messages in scripture that only the Spirit in the reader can extract, and "Augustine called the Bible 'Letters from home'" {{PKB-EX-1981-LETTERSHOME}}. And it is incomplete. The same Exegesis that calls the Bible code insists that Acts as canonised leaves out what Flow My Tears preserves {{PKB-EX-1976-OMITS}}. By 1981 Dick reads his own novels as two ciphers in opposite directions: Flow My Tears political on the surface with a hidden stream from Acts and Daniel, VALIS theological on the surface with a hidden political one {{PKB-LET-1981-REVERSE}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Living scripture
body: Early in 1975 Dick thought the Bible was dispensable: suppress it entirely and the experience it records would "spring to life within given human minds once more" {{PKB-LET-1975-WILLIAMS}}. He ended in the opposite place. Copying out Philo's image of the Torah as a living being, body the literal text and soul the hidden meaning, he exclaims: "This is the Acts material, the living information I saw" {{PKB-EX-1978-TORAH}}. Elsewhere he is "sure that the plasmate" is "the Living Torah, the informational basis of reality" {{PKB-EX-1978-LIVINGTORAH}}.

The organism is also a world. Already in November 1975 "The world of the Bible was suddenly around me, and real, replacing our world" {{PKB-EX-1975-WORLDOFBIBLE}}. Later entries say Valis turned the Bible's information into our world {{PKB-EX-1978-TEMPLATE}}, picture the Bible in three dimensions, its layers ordered by age {{PKB-EX-1978-THREED}}, and arrive in April 1981 at the formula: "the Bible is not a verbal description of a world; it is a world" {{PKB-EX-1981-ISAWORLD}}. It is the touchstone for every other theory {{PKB-EX-1981-TOUCHSTONE}}. To Patricia Warrick he wrote that the Bible is "the information that is fed into the space-time universe", and that a single life form underlies it, "not fixed into a canon" {{PKB-LET-1981-SOURCE}} {{PKB-LET-1981-LIFEFORM}}.

The carriers of this living text are manuscripts that came out of the ground. Thomas, the personality he believed took him over, slumbered "perhaps in a jar at Qumran" {{PKB-EX-1976-QUMRAN}}; the huge open books he saw were the Qumran scrolls Bishop Pike saw, passed to him as plasmate {{PKB-EX-1978-SCROLLS}}; the Nag Hammadi codices may be "the actual Secret Living" blood of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-NAGHAMMADI}}. The Logos of John's prologue is the bridge between text and organism, and Ubik's "I am the word" is the proof he finds in his own fiction {{PKB-EX-1978-UBIKWORD}}.

The novels build the idea as objects. Elias's holographic Bible in The Divine Invasion yields different messages at every angle, "an infinitude of knowledge that ceaselessly changed" {{PKB-FIC-DI-HOLOGRAM}}, until it becomes "a sentient organism that was never twice the same" {{PKB-FIC-DI-SENTIENT}}; Elias defines the Torah as alive and prior to creation {{PKB-FIC-DI-TORAHDEF}}; Zina declares "I am the Torah" {{PKB-FIC-DI-TORAH}}. Tseng reads the open, living scripture against the novel's Church, which wants to freeze it {{PKB-SCH-TSENG}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Recombinant scripture and a third testament
body: If scripture is alive, it can grow. Reading Joachim of Fiore's three ages, Dick concluded that the third is as revolutionary against the Christian age as that was against the first: "New Scriptures are needed, new prophets and perhaps a new savior" {{PKB-EX-1978-NEWSCRIPTURES}}.

By 1981 he had a name for what replaces a closed canon. "Recombinant scripture" has "no canon, no precedent; each person + situation unique" {{PKB-EX-1981-RECOMBINANT}}; to Patricia Warrick, a message "applies to one person for one situation only" and is then scrapped {{PKB-LET-1981-RECOMBINANT}}. The same month in the Exegesis he speaks of an "unprecedented third testament emanating out of the O.T. + N.T." {{PKB-EX-1981-THIRDTESTAMENT}}. The Divine Invasion stages the temptation and the restraint: Emmanuel wants to add a line to the hologram of the Bible and knows he should not {{PKB-FIC-DI-ADDENDUM}}.

dossier_sections.heading: The Torah, and a turn to Judaism
body: In February 1975 Dick had little use for the Hebrew Bible: "All the O.T. has in it is monotheism, which they got from Iknaton" {{PKB-EX-1975-IKHNATON}}. Five years later, researching the sequel to VALIS with J. H. Hertz's edition of the Pentateuch, he equated the Torah with the Holy Wisdom of Proverbs 8 {{PKB-LET-1980-HERTZ}}.

The interviews from these years go further. He made "a very detailed study of the Torah and the basic tenets of Judaism" for The Divine Invasion {{PKB-INT-TORAHSTUDY}}; he reads Deuteronomy with Hertz's notes and marvels at its care for the poor {{PKB-INT-DEUTERONOMY}}; he says outright "I've switched from Christianity to Judaism" {{PKB-INT-SWITCHED}} — and, in another conversation, that he studied the Torah until he understood it, "snuck in some Christianity" and "finally got back to Christianity" {{PKB-INT-STUDIEDTORAH}}. To Ursula K. Le Guin in August 1981 the Torah's "haunting concern for all creatures" is what enchants him {{PKB-LET-1981-LEGUIN}}.

The Exegesis keeps the two in tension rather than choosing. Jesus was rejected, Dick argues, "Because he depreciated the Torah" — and only God's Wisdom could claim that authority {{PKB-EX-1978-DEPRECIATED}}. In April 1981, in the Hamlet allegory where the Torah is the usurping king: "Torah does not know everything. Christ does." {{PKB-EX-1981-TORAHCHRIST}}

dossier_sections.heading: Which Bible: translations and editions
body: Dick did not read one Bible. The archive shows him using at least five, and paying attention to their differences: the King James, whose cadence he took for granted {{PKB-LET-1964}} and a copy of which he gave his mother {{PKB-EX-1978-KJV}}; the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation, which he preferred in 1973 {{PKB-LET-1973C}} and whose reading of Daniel he borrowed {{PKB-EX-1975-CLAYFEET}} while rejecting its theology of Christ {{PKB-EX-1978-MATTHEW}}; the New English Bible, which he quotes for John 10 {{PKB-LET-1975-KORMAN}} and checks for the word "secret" in 1 Corinthians 2 {{PKB-EX-1981-SECRET}}; the Jerusalem Bible, "an official Catholic Bible", whose notes he was already citing in 1975 {{PKB-EX-1975-JBIBLE}} and studies in 1981 {{PKB-LET-1981-BLOODWATER}} {{PKB-LET-1981-AGAPE}}; and Jerome's Vulgate, the source of the word he wanted on his gravestone, Dilexi {{PKB-LET-DILEXI}}. From 1980 a sixth joins them: Hertz's Hebrew-English Pentateuch, with its commentary {{PKB-LET-1980-HERTZ}} {{PKB-INT-STUDIEDTORAH}}.

He also read through intermediaries: the Septuagint's apocrypha {{PKB-EX-1975-SEPTUAGINT}}, The Decoded New Testament's esoteric glosses on the Crucifixion {{PKB-EX-1975-DECODED}}, and reference books on Exodus when a television drama got Passover wrong {{PKB-LET-1975-CBS}}. The last novel's bibliography cites the Jerusalem Bible, and its narrator notices the change of translation in a bishop's hands {{PKB-FIC-ARCHER-DIM}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Which God?
body: Dick never decided which God of the Bible he had met, and his answers are incompatible. In 1977 he tells Julian Jaynes it was "not so much the creator god of our Bible" as Plato's arranger {{PKB-LET-1977-JAYNES}}. Reading the Nag Hammadi codices, he concludes that Palmer Eldritch, explicitly the Christian God of that novel, is the Gnostics' blind demiurge {{PKB-EX-1978-YALTABAOTH}}. Late in 1980 it is the Cosmic Christ of John, distinct from the human Jesus, and its nature is agape {{PKB-EX-1980-COSMICCHRIST}}; in the same entry Proverbs 8 costs him his doctrine of the Trinity: "herewith I just lost my Trinitarianism" {{PKB-EX-1980-TRINITARIANISM}}.

In April 1981 he reverses that: the king on horseback in the Tears dream is YHWH, judge and destroyer, "not the God of the N.T., the Xtian God of agape" but the God whom Moses knew, and VALIS is "a fusion of Exodus & Daniel" {{PKB-EX-1981-YHWH}}. Two years earlier the same figure was the young king, Christ as judge, of Daniel and Revelation {{PKB-EX-1978-YOUNGKING}}. The last novel gives the question to scholarship: the mysterious word in the Zadokite scrolls is anokhi, God's "I" in Exodus 20 {{PKB-FIC-ARCHER-ANOKHI}}.

dossier_sections.heading: Scripture in the novels
body: The fiction uses the Bible in two ways, and the difference matters. Overtly, characters quote and argue: Pete in Deus Irae calls the Bible "a chronicle of God's search for man" {{PKB-FIC-DEUSIRAE}}; Fat's journal is an exegesis because it treats his revelations as scripture {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-EXEGESIS}}; Bob Arctor understands the "glass darkly" verse and cannot be helped by it {{PKB-FIC-SCANNER}}. In VALIS Sherri asks whether a parable in Luke is one of "the corrupt parts of the Bible" {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-CORRUPT}}, and Fat traces Psalm 104 to Ikhnaton's hymn {{PKB-FIC-VALIS-PSALM}} — the Exegesis' claim of 1975, given to a character. These are characters speaking, not Dick.

The short stories reach for the Bible as ordinary speech: whether a strange light is God, "like in the Bible" {{PKB-FIC-STORY-TERRAN}}; a Bible bound in wub-fur that rewrites Corinthians {{PKB-FIC-STORY-WUB}}; a dream of huge open books, "Even holy, like the Bible" {{PKB-FIC-STORY-SIBYL}}, which anticipates the Exegesis' open books; scripture cited as authority {{PKB-FIC-STORY-RETREAT}} and as resignation {{PKB-FIC-STORY-TEMPUNAUTS}}.

Covertly, on Dick's own later account, the novels carried scripture he did not know he had put there — Acts in Flow My Tears, the Logos in Ubik. That is a claim about the novels made from outside them, and the page keeps it in Dick's lane, not the fiction's. He could also turn on his own scripture-quoting characters: rereading The Transmigration of Timothy Archer, he decided its bishop uses the Bible "not as a man of God but as a lawyer" {{PKB-LET-1981-ARCHER}}.

dossier_sections.heading: What scholars say
body: Sutin places the Bible and the Dead Sea Scrolls in a lifelong, "virtually limitless" range of reading {{PKB-SCH-SUTIN-01}}. Butler makes 1 Corinthians a standing heading in his survey of every novel {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-02}}, traces Felix and Jason to Acts 17 {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-03}}, and states that Dick had not previously read Acts {{PKB-SCH-BUTLER-01}}. An essay in Theory, Culture & Society reads the "glass, darkly" verse and its sequel, caritas, as the two halves of Dick's late thought {{PKB-SCH-TCS-01}}, and points to work comparing Paul's conversion in Acts 9 with February 1974 {{PKB-SCH-TCS-02}}. Tseng and the Extrapolation essay read The Divine Invasion's open Bible and its Job-like wager {{PKB-SCH-TSENG}} {{PKB-SCH-EXTRAP}}.

dossier_sections.heading: What this page does not claim
body: It does not claim that Dick's scriptural readings are correct, or that the coincidences he found in Flow My Tears are more than coincidences. It reports what he wrote and what others have written, in separate lanes: the fiction is characters speaking, the Exegesis and letters are Dick, the scholarship is scholars.

Dates are given per passage with the evidence for them. Exegesis section 016 carries a container date of October 1978 that its own passages contradict; passages from it are dated 1978–80 unless a stamp or folder places them more precisely. The 348 machine-extracted "claims" about the Bible in our database are unreviewed and are not used here; every card on this page was chosen and summarised by reading the passage, and every quotation is checked verbatim against its source before the page is built.

Fifty of the cards were first written for a separate study, The Bible in PKD (October 2026), built without access to the full letters and texts. They were merged here after each was re-anchored to its full source; where the sources disagreed with that study, they were followed — the rhymed-couplets letter, for instance, is to Patrice Duvic on 28 November 1972, not to Roger Zelazny, and the "I had never read Acts" entry dates from mid-1978, not September 1976.

mention_cards.citation: Interview with Gregg Rickman, in Philip K. Dick: The Last Interview and Other Conversations
mention_cards.context: Asked by Gregg Rickman where his religious preoccupations come from, Dick goes back to junior high school and a daytime radio serial, The Light of the World, that dramatised the Bible. He tuned in during the Elijah episodes, then read the story for himself, and wanted above everything to hear the low murmuring voice Elijah hears on Mount Horeb. He says he heard such a voice two or three years later, during an eleventh-grade physics exam — and then, half-mocking, files the whole account as an enormous fantasy. It is the earliest date he ever gives for reading scripture, and it ties the Bible to the voice, not to doctrine.
mention_cards.pith: And I started reading the Bible and I read that part about Elijah.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick's own retrospective account, given in the last year of his life. Sutin independently records a Bible Club he tried to found in junior high (PKB-SCH-SUTIN-02).
mention_cards.passage: … When I was a kid—here’s your psychological theory. I will give you all the ammunition you need here for your “reductive psychological”— **RICKMAN :** It’s a theory. I didn’t say I believed it. [ _Laughter_ ] **DICK :** When I was in junior high school there was a soap opera on daytime radio called _The Light of the World_ , a story of the Bible. They dramatized part of the Bible. I happened to start listening during the part about Elijah. And I started reading the Bible and I read that part about Elijah. And it was my greatest wish in the world of anything to hear that low murmuring voice that Elijah heard. The voice of the Lord and that is the etiology of that psychologically.
